name: a-two-colour-overhead
prompt: Tall upright weekly-magazine plate from 1919, pulled on a letterpress in only two inks on warm cream stock: a black key drawing, with one flat brick-red (#A63A2B) laid over it as a separate plate and nudged a hair out of register. The viewpoint perches at the crown of an iron lamp standard and stares almost straight down at a park bench in deep winter. Bench, raked gravel walk and the stretched shadows of leafless plane trees all run together in one hard slant from bottom left to top right, splitting the page in two. At the bench's left end, foreshortened from above, sits an enormous round plutocrat: the glossy black disc of his topper, sloping coat shoulders, a starched wing collar, and bulging between his lapels a waistcoat that holds the only red anywhere on the plate, its flat red sprinkled with rows of minute dollar signs. One gloved arm swings outward, away from his neighbour, palm flicking the air the way you would shoo off a waiter. At the far end, empty slats gaping between them, a gaunt demobbed private hunches in a shabby army greatcoat and field cap; his left leg stops at the knee, the empty khaki pinned up flat, his right foot in a hobnailed boot planted on the gravel, a rough ash-wood crutch leaning beside him. Low winter sun stretches the crutch and that lone boot into two long, thin black shadows that stripe across the walk by themselves. Brisk dip-pen line, ruled parallel hatching in the shade, solid black on hat and coats; the red has no outline of its own; faint ink spread and visible paper tooth. The top fifth of the sheet stays bare cream paper, nothing drawn there at all. No lettering, words, monograms or speech balloons anywhere on the plate. Thanks.
